rite_divergence.desc:
Divergence measures how far a Rite's Tenets and Doctrines have drifted from the parent Faith. A Rite that adopts Prohibited Tenets as Core is more Divergent.

High Divergence weakens the parent faith's Fervor making outbreaks of Heresy more common. A Rite that reaches 100 Divergence will be automatically declared a heresy and become a new Faith.

tenet_status.desc:
Tenet Status is a Rite's stance on a Tenet or Doctrine. There are five possible stances:

• Unknown — the Rite has never heard of this Tenet or Doctrine.

• Known — the Rite is aware of it and has not ruled on its practice.

• Permitted — the Rite approves of the practice.

• Prohibited — the Rite forbids the practice.

• Core — the Rite both permits and actively promotes the Tenet.

A Rite's stance governs whether a Tenet or Doctrine can be picked when authoring or diverging a Rite, and which practices cost adherents spiritual penalties.

Tenet Status is distinct from a Character's Religious Knowledge, which is personal awareness, not the overall Rite's stance.

glossary.text:
Hesychasm, from Greek hēsykhía meaning stillness, is a contemplative tradition in Eastern Christianity emphasizing prayer of the heart, rooted in the 4th century Desert Fathers of Egypt. Its central practice became the repeated Jesus Prayer, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner, often coordinated with one's breathing and heartbeat.

In the 14th century, Saint Gregory Palamas defended the Hesychast monks of Mount Athos, and their visions of the uncreated Light of Tabor of the Transfiguration, against charges of heresy by Barlaam of Calabria. Councils at Constantinople in 1341 and 1351 vindicated Palamas and established Hesychasm as Orthodox doctrine.

glossary.text:
Monasticism spread throughout the Catholic world during the Middle Ages, with monasteries established across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. Monks and nuns took vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, living either as hermits in isolated cells or in communal houses under strict rules.

These institutions served multiple functions: preserving manuscripts and classical texts, providing education, operating hospitals and hospices, managing agricultural estates, and offering hospitality to travelers. Monastic orders like the Benedictines, Cistercians, and Carthusians each developed distinct traditions regarding prayer, work, and community life.

Monastic communities exist across many religious traditions, not only Christianity but also Buddhism, Hinduism, and Jainism. These institutions typically involve individuals withdrawing from ordinary society to pursue religious devotion through prayer, meditation, study, and ascetic practices.

Monasteries often function as centers of learning, preserving sacred texts and providing education. They may be completely isolated from the surrounding population or maintain active engagement through charitable works, medical care, and agricultural production. The specific rules governing monastic life vary widely between traditions and individual communities.
